name: Drotaverine + Mefenamic Acid
meta: Drotaverine 80 mg + Mefenamic acid 250 mg (strength not stated in product list –
Drotaverine Hydrochloride: Antispasmodic (phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor); Mefenamic Acid: NSAID (fenamate)
Drotaverine Hydrochloride: A03AD02; Mefenamic Acid: M01AG01
Schedule H – prescription only; Mefenamic Acid: Schedule H – prescription only
sections: White to greyish-white microcrystalline powder, practically insoluble in water.

Drotaverine Hydrochloride: A papaverine analogue widely used in Europe and Asia for smooth-muscle spasm; not available in the USA. First approval/introduction: Introduced 1961 (Chinoin, Hungary). Mefenamic Acid: A fenamate (anthranilic acid) NSAID particularly used for dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia. First approval/introduction: Invented 1961 (Claude Winder, Parke-Davis); US marketing 1967.
Drotaverine 80 mg + Mefenamic acid 250 mg (strength not stated in product list –
Drotaverine relaxes smooth-muscle spasm without anticholinergic effects; mefenamic acid inhibits prostaglandins that drive uterine contraction and pain. Combined antispasmodic and analgesic action.

Drotaverine Hydrochloride Inhibits PDE-4, increasing cAMP in smooth muscle and causing relaxation of GI, biliary, urogenital and uterine smooth muscle without anticholinergic effects. Receptor / target profile: Selective PDE-4 inhibitor raising cAMP, reducing intracellular calcium and relaxing smooth muscle; no anticholinergic activity.

Mefenamic Acid Inhibits COX and antagonises prostaglandin receptors; reduces uterine prostaglandins, relieving dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia. Receptor / target profile: Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 and antagonises prostaglandin receptors.
Summary: Bioavailability 25–91%; Tmax 45–60 min. Highly protein bound. Hepatic metabolism. Half-life 7–12 h.
Summary: Tmax 2–4 h; >90% protein bound; metabolised by CYP2C9. Half-life ~2 h.
Abdominal colic – intestinal, biliary, renal/ureteric colic
One tablet three times daily after food
Dysmenorrhoea: start at onset of pain/menses, for 2–3 days
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Tablets: ≥1 year at reduced dose per some labels.
Avoid in pregnancy unless clearly needed.
Avoid in severe impairment (CrCl <30); monitor creatinine in mild–moderate impairment.
Avoid in severe impairment; use lowest dose in mild–moderate.
Higher risk of GI bleeding, renal impairment and CV events – lowest dose, shortest time; consider gastroprotection (PPI).
Not recommended under 14 years (some labels allow ≥6 months for fever at specialist discretion).
Severe hepatic, renal or cardiac failure (low output)
Hypersensitivity, or asthma/urticaria/rhinitis triggered by aspirin or other NSAIDs
Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; history of recurrent ulceration
Cardiovascular thrombotic events (MI, stroke) – use lowest dose for shortest time
GI ulceration, bleeding and perforation – higher risk in elderly, with steroids, anticoagulants, SSRIs
Hepatotoxicity – monitor LFTs on long-term use
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics (reduced effect, renal impairment)
Drotaverine Hydrochloride: With or without food.
Mefenamic Acid: Take after food or with milk; avoid alcohol (GI bleeding).
Mefenamic Acid: BP, renal function, LFTs and CBC on prolonged use; signs of GI bleeding.
Drotaverine Hydrochloride: Arrhythmias, AV block; supportive care. Mefenamic Acid: Seizures, GI symptoms; supportive care.
Cochrane review (Marjoribanks et al., 2015) – NSAIDs including mefenamic acid effective for primary dysmenorrhoea.
Small Indian randomised trials report benefit of the combination in dysmenorrhoea and colic.
Do not combine with other painkillers containing NSAIDs
Report black stools, vomiting blood, chest pain, swelling
Use for the shortest time needed
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
